blocks.content: Picture the backend for an online store. One codebase handles catalog browsing, cart, checkout, and payments. It's all one app, one repo, one deploy.

Six months in, three teams are pushing changes into that same repo. A typo in the payment module blocks the catalog team's release. A traffic spike during a sale means you scale the entire app, even the parts that see almost no extra traffic.
That specific kind of pain, teams blocking each other and unable to scale just the busy part, is what pushes companies toward microservices.
Microservices means splitting one application into a set of small, independently deployable services, each owning its own data and a narrow slice of the business.
1. Introduction

This topic is about the shape of the architecture, not any single tool. You will see the term a lot in interviews, usually as "would you use microservices here, and why." The honest answer is almost always "it depends," and this topic gives you the reasoning to back that up.

blocks.title: Scope
blocks.content: Service discovery and API gateways get their own topics. Here we only touch them enough to explain how split-up services find each other.
2. What Microservices Actually Are

A microservice is a small application in its own right. It runs as its own process, it can be deployed on its own, and it talks to other services only over the network, usually HTTP or a message queue. Nothing about it is shared code that gets imported directly into another service.
2.1 Independently deployable

This is the part people skip past, and it's the whole point. If you can't ship the orders service on Tuesday without also redeploying catalog and payment, you don't really have microservices yet, no matter how many repos you've split the code into.

blocks.title: Common trap
blocks.content: Splitting code into separate folders or even separate repos doesn't make it a microservice. If two services still need to deploy together to work, they're one deployment unit wearing two costumes.
2.2 Owns its own data

Each service gets its own database, or at minimum its own set of tables that nothing else touches directly. The orders service never runs a SQL join against the payment service's tables. If it needs payment data, it asks the payment service for it.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396266847-140029749.png
blocks.alt: Three services, catalog, orders, and payment, each connected only to its own private database

blocks.content: This is what actually buys you independent deploys. If services shared a database, changing one table's schema could break three services at once, and you'd be back to coordinating releases.
2.3 Owns a narrow business capability

Good service boundaries map to a business capability like "manage the catalog" or "process payments," not to a technical layer like "the database access code." We come back to this in detail in section 5, since getting it wrong is the single most expensive mistake in this whole topic.
2.4 Monolith vs microservices, side by side

3. Why Teams Move to Microservices
None of these reasons are about microservices being newer or fancier. Each one is a specific pain a monolith causes once you cross a certain size, in traffic or in team headcount.
3.1 Independent scaling of hot services

In an online store, catalog browsing gets ten times the traffic that checkout does. In a monolith, scaling means running more copies of the entire app, catalog code, checkout code, and all, just to handle catalog load. Wasteful, but you have no choice since it's all one process.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396266848-696388097.png
blocks.alt: A load balancer sending traffic to three catalog instances but only one payment instance

blocks.content: Split into services, and you run ten catalog instances and one payment instance. You pay for the capacity you actually need, where you actually need it.
3.2 Independent deploys per team

When each team owns a service end to end, code, database, deploy pipeline, and on call, they ship on their own schedule. The catalog team can push five times a day. The payment team, dealing with a stricter compliance process, can push once a week. Neither blocks the other.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396266848-528899919.png
blocks.alt: One team owning a payment service's code, database, deploy pipeline, and on call rotation

blocks.content: 3.3 Technology choice per service

A recommendation engine might genuinely be faster to build in Python because of the machine learning libraries available. A payment service might want the stricter typing of a statically typed language. In a monolith you're stuck with one language and one runtime for everything. With services, each team picks what fits their problem.

blocks.title: Keep this in perspective
blocks.content: Technology freedom sounds exciting but running five languages across ten services also means five sets of tooling, five sets of on call runbooks, and five things to hire for. Most companies deliberately limit themselves to two or three stacks even after adopting microservices.
3.4 Fault isolation

If the recommendation engine crashes in a monolith, depending on how tangled the code is, it can take checkout down with it. As a separate service, a crash there means users just stop seeing recommendations. Checkout keeps working.

blocks.title: A concrete failure
blocks.text: During a flash sale, the review service starts timing out because a badly written query locks a table. In a monolith, every request touching that shared process slows down or fails, including checkout. As a separate service behind a timeout and a fallback, the product page just quietly hides the reviews section and checkout is unaffected.

blocks.content: 4. The Real Costs

This is the section interviewers actually care about. Anyone can list the benefits of microservices. Knowing the costs, in specific terms, is what shows you've actually thought about the trade off instead of repeating a buzzword.
4.1 A network call replaces a function call
blocks.text: 4.1 A network call replaces a function call

blocks.content: In a monolith, the checkout code calling the payment code is a function call. It takes microseconds, it can't time out, and it can't fail because a network cable got unplugged. Once payment becomes a separate service, that same call goes over HTTP or a queue.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396266849-169267669.png
blocks.alt: The same call to payment logic, an in process function call in a monolith versus a network call in microservices

blocks.content: Now that call can be slow, can time out, can fail halfway through, and needs retries, timeouts, and a plan for what happens if payment simply doesn't answer.
4.2 Distributed transactions become hard

Placing an order in a monolith with one database is a single transaction. Reserve the stock, charge the card, save the order, all commit together or all roll back together. Spread across services with separate databases, there is no single transaction anymore.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396266850-266267885.png
blocks.alt: Orders service calling inventory to reserve stock and payment to charge a card, with payment failing

blocks.content: If the payment call fails after inventory already reserved stock, you're left with reserved stock and no paid order. Fixing this needs patterns like sagas or compensating actions, which is real design work that a monolith simply never asked you to do.
4.3 Operational complexity multiplies

Ten services means ten things to deploy, ten things to monitor, ten sets of logs, and ten places a bad config can break something. You now need service discovery, centralized logging, distributed tracing, and a deploy pipeline that can handle far more moving pieces than a single app ever did.

["One service down at 3am used to mean one thing to check, now it can mean checking which of ten services is actually the problem","A config change that used to be one file is now potentially ten files, one per service","Local development, running the whole system on your laptop, gets genuinely harder as the service count grows"]
items: One service down at 3am used to mean one thing to check, now it can mean checking which of ten services is actually the problem
A config change that used to be one file is now potentially ten files, one per service
Local development, running the whole system on your laptop, gets genuinely harder as the service count grows

blocks.content: 4.4 Debugging across services is harder

A single slow checkout request might touch the API gateway, the cart service, the orders service, and the payment service. Without tooling, you're grepping through four separate log files trying to line up timestamps to figure out where the fifteen seconds went.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396269865-377558835.png
blocks.alt: One request flowing through an API gateway, cart, orders, and payment services in sequence

blocks.title: What actually fixes this
blocks.content: A request id generated at the gateway and passed through every downstream call, combined with centralized logging and distributed tracing. Without that in place from day one, debugging across services becomes genuinely painful, not just theoretically harder.
4.5 Data consistency needs deliberate design

When the catalog service updates a product's price, the cart service might have already cached that price for items sitting in someone's cart. In a monolith with one database, that inconsistency doesn't exist since there's only one copy of the truth. Across services, you have to decide, explicitly, how stale each copy of the data is allowed to be, and how it eventually catches up.
5. Drawing Service Boundaries
Get the boundaries wrong and you end up with the worst of both worlds, all the network overhead of microservices with none of the independence they were supposed to buy you.
5.1 Around business capabilities, not technical layers
blocks.text: 5.1 Around business capabilities, not technical layers

blocks.content: A tempting but wrong split is by technical layer, a UI service, a business logic service, a data access service. That's wrong because a single feature change, say adding a discount code, now touches all three services and needs all three deployed together. You've gained nothing over a monolith except extra network hops.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396269865-153506996.png
blocks.alt: A wrong split into UI, business logic, and data layers next to a correct orders service owning its full slice

blocks.content: The right split is by business capability. An orders service owns everything about placing and tracking orders: its own logic, its own data, its own API. A single feature change to how orders work usually stays inside that one service.
5.2 A quick test for a boundary
blocks.text: 5.2 A quick test for a boundary

blocks.content: ["Can this service be described in one sentence without the word \"and\"? \"Manages the catalog\" is good, \"manages the catalog and handles checkout\" means split it further","Does most of a typical feature change stay inside this one service? If features constantly need two services changed together, the boundary is probably in the wrong place","Could a small team own this service completely, including its data, without waiting on another team?"]
items: Can this service be described in one sentence without the word "and"? "Manages the catalog" is good, "manages the catalog and handles checkout" means split it further
Does most of a typical feature change stay inside this one service? If features constantly need two services changed together, the boundary is probably in the wrong place
Could a small team own this service completely, including its data, without waiting on another team?

blocks.content: 6. How Services Find and Talk to Each Other
blocks.text: 6. How Services Find and Talk to Each Other

blocks.content: Once you have separate services, something has to know where each one lives, since instances get added, removed, and restarted all the time, often with changing network addresses.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396269866-89644112.png
blocks.alt: A client hitting an API gateway, which checks a service registry before forwarding to the target service

blocks.content: A service registry keeps track of which instances of a service are alive and where they are. An API gateway usually sits in front of everything, giving clients one address to call while it figures out internally which service should actually handle the request.

blocks.title: Going deeper
blocks.content: Service discovery and API gateways are both big enough topics on their own, covered separately. The one thing to remember here is that this routing layer is not optional once you have more than a couple of services, someone or something has to do this job.
7. The Premature Decomposition Trap

The single most common way teams get microservices wrong is splitting too early. A five person team building a brand new product does not have the scaling problems or the team coordination problems that microservices exist to solve. Splitting anyway just adds network calls and deploy complexity to a codebase that didn't need either yet.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396269866-129203208.png
blocks.alt: Three tightly coupled services calling each other in a circle, all shown in red

blocks.content: What usually happens is the boundaries get drawn based on guesses, not real usage patterns, since the product hasn't existed long enough to reveal where the real seams are. The services end up needing to change together constantly anyway, calling each other back and forth in circles. You end up with a distributed monolith, all the deployment pain of separate services with none of the independence.
If your services can't be deployed, scaled, or changed independently in practice, you haven't built microservices. You've built a monolith with extra network hops and extra failure modes.

blocks.title: A better default
blocks.content: Start with a well organized monolith, with clear internal module boundaries. Split a module out into its own service once it has a real, specific reason: it needs to scale differently, a team needs to own it independently, or it needs a different tech stack. Let the pain point tell you where to cut, don't guess up front.

blocks.content: 9. The Interview Angle
When an interviewer asks whether you'd use microservices for a design, they're testing whether you can justify the split with a real reason, not whether you know the word.
9.1 Justify with scaling and team reasons, not trends
blocks.text: 9.1 Justify with scaling and team reasons, not trends

blocks.content: "Microservices are more modern" or "microservices are what big companies use" are answers that will lose you points. Instead, point at something specific in the problem: a component that clearly needs to scale differently, a team boundary that keeps causing deploy conflicts, or a component with genuinely different reliability or compliance requirements.

blocks.title: A strong interview answer
blocks.text: "I'd keep this as a monolith at first since we're describing a single small team and moderate traffic. If the notification sending piece later becomes a bottleneck under load, or if a separate team takes ownership of it, that's when I'd pull it out into its own service, since at that point it has a specific reason to be independent."

blocks.content: 9.2 Mistakes that stand out for the wrong reason

blocks.content: 10. Summary
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396269867-564744287.png
blocks.alt: A decision flow, staying a monolith by default, splitting only when there's clear scaling or team pain

blocks.content: Microservices trade simplicity for independence: independent scaling, independent deploys, and fault isolation, at the cost of network calls, distributed transactions, and real operational overhead. None of that trade is free, and none of it is automatically worth it.

blocks.title: The one line to remember
blocks.content: Default to a monolith. Split out a service only when a specific, real pain, scaling, team ownership, or compliance, points at it. Boundaries follow business capabilities, never technical layers.
